title: What they said at the time

clips.q: When business gets bad enough, a company will try just about anything.
We are aware that some blacks find our name insensitive, but we have a legal right to retain the name and plan to do so.
clips.who: **David Severson**, Sambo’s spokesman, The New York Times, Nov 18, 1978[^1]

clips.q: We are taking this step to improve our market position in New England.
clips.who: **Arthur K. Dowd**, on renaming 18 restaurants, The Christian Science Monitor, Apr 22, 1981[^5]

clips.q: We asked them to change the name, and they have complied.
clips.who: **Abner Darby**, New England president of the NAACP, The Christian Science Monitor, Apr 22, 1981[^5]

clips.q: This case raises novel freedom of speech issues regarding the standard for the waiver of first amendment rights and the scope of first amendment protection to be afforded “offensive” commercial speech.
clips.who: **Judge Anthony J. Celebrezze**, Sambo’s Restaurants v. City of Ann Arbor, Nov 4, 1981[^12]

clips.q: Sambo’s Restaurants Inc., once a rapidly growing and highly regarded chain of coffee shops, is now in deep trouble, its survival threatened.
clips.who: **Robert Metz**, Market Place, The New York Times, Nov 27, 1981[^9]

clips.q: We shot ourselves in the foot in 1985, pushing too many people into outlying Sambo’s locations, which proved non-viable.
clips.who: **Robert S. Benson**, president of Vicorp, in Nation’s Restaurant News, 1989, as quoted in a reference history[^15]

clips.q: My main goal a year ago was to change the name.
clips.who: **Chad Stevens**, before deciding to keep it, Los Angeles Times, Jan 12, 1998[^18]

clips.q: There is no way that they cannot know that this is problematic.
clips.who: **Jeffrey T. Sammons**, professor of history, New York University, Los Angeles Times, Jan 12, 1998[^18]

clips.q: Our family has looked into our hearts and realize that we must be sensitive when others whom we respect make a strong appeal.
clips.who: **The owners’ statement**, June 2020, as quoted by NBC News[^25]
